questions.stem: Prohibition in the USA, introduced by the Eighteenth Amendment and in force from 1920, banned:
options: the import of foreign films and jazz recordings
the sale of tobacco to anyone under twenty-one
the making, sale and transport of alcohol
the drinking of alcohol inside private homes
questions.explanation: Prohibition outlawed the manufacture, sale and transport of intoxicating liquor, but drinking it was not itself a crime. This gap helped speakeasies and bootleggers flourish.

questions.stem: Which was an unintended consequence of Prohibition in the USA?
options: a permanent end to drinking in American cities
the loss of women's right to vote in federal elections
a large rise in federal tax revenue from beer and spirits
the growth of organised crime and bootlegging
questions.explanation: Gangsters such as Al Capone made fortunes supplying illegal alcohol, and corruption spread through police and city governments. The government actually lost the tax revenue that legal alcohol had provided, and Prohibition was repealed in 1933.

questions.stem: How did Henry Ford's moving assembly line change American society by the 1920s?
options: it made cars cheap enough for many ordinary families
it ended the use of wage labour in American factories
it moved most car production from the cities to farming towns
it made skilled craftsmen more important than ever in industry
questions.explanation: Mass production cut the price of the Model T so far that car ownership spread to millions of households, changing work, leisure and where people lived. It reduced, rather than increased, the need for skilled craftsmen.

questions.stem: In the USA in the 1920s, 'flappers' were:
options: female inspectors appointed to check conditions in factories
young women who defied convention in dress and behaviour
rural women who campaigned to keep Prohibition in force
workers who led the national strikes for an eight-hour day
questions.explanation: Flappers wore short hair and short skirts, smoked, drank and danced to jazz, challenging older ideas of how respectable women behaved. Critics saw them as a symbol of the decade's new personal freedoms.

questions.stem: In 1920 the Nineteenth Amendment to the US Constitution:
options: gave women the right to vote
abolished segregated public schools
banned the sale of alcohol nationally
first gave African American men the vote
questions.explanation: The Nineteenth Amendment barred denying the vote on the basis of sex. African American men had been given the vote by the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870, though southern states used other laws to stop most of them using it.

questions.stem: Which development in the USA in the 1930s best shows change to workers' rights?
options: the Nineteenth Amendment extending the vote to all women
the Wagner Act of 1935 protecting the right to join unions
the Volstead Act enforcing the national ban on alcohol
the Plessy v Ferguson ruling on separate public facilities
questions.explanation: The Wagner Act, part of the New Deal, protected workers' right to organise and bargain collectively, and union membership grew rapidly. The other laws and rulings concerned alcohol, segregation and suffrage, and came earlier.

questions.stem: Japan's moga, or Modern Girls, of the 1920s were criticised as a challenge to:
options: the ideal of the 'good wife, wise mother'
the democratic reforms of the Meiji Constitution
the army's control of the government in Tokyo
the Buddhist priesthood's control over schooling
questions.explanation: Moga with bobbed hair and Western clothes who worked in offices and cafes seemed to reject the official ideal that women's role was to serve family and nation in the home. They became a symbol of the urban, consumer culture of the Taisho period.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 gave most women the vote in federal elections, but it:
options: applied only to women who owned land or property
applied only to women who were over the age of thirty
excluded most Aboriginal people from voting
did not let women stand as candidates for Parliament
questions.explanation: The Act let women vote and stand for federal Parliament, but it barred 'aboriginal natives' of Australia, Asia, Africa and the Pacific Islands (except New Zealand) unless already enrolled in a state. Aboriginal people did not gain full federal voting rights until 1962.

questions.stem: In Britain, the Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to:
options: only those women who had served in the armed forces
every woman except those married to serving soldiers
women over 30 who met a property qualification
all women over 21 on exactly the same terms as men
questions.explanation: The 1918 Act gave the vote to women over 30 who met property conditions, along with almost all men over 21. Women gained the vote on equal terms with men only in 1928.

questions.stem: Which Nazi measure from 1933 was designed to encourage German women to marry and have more children?
options: free university places for married women
laws giving women equal pay in factories
a ban on women joining any Nazi organisation
marriage loans reduced for each child born
questions.explanation: Couples received a loan when the wife gave up paid work, and a quarter of it was cancelled with each child. Nazi ideology saw motherhood as women's duty to the nation, so equal pay and university places were not encouraged.

questions.stem: Which change in Stalin's USSR in 1936 marked a retreat from the early Bolsheviks' policies on women and the family?
options: women were banned from working in heavy industry factories
the state opened its first creches for working mothers
abortion was banned again and divorce made harder
women gained the right to vote for the very first time
questions.explanation: The Bolsheviks had legalised abortion and made divorce easy in the early 1920s, but Stalin's 1936 decree reversed this to strengthen the family and raise the birth rate. Women had the vote from 1917 and were encouraged into industrial work throughout the 1930s.

questions.stem: Collectivisation of Soviet agriculture from 1929 meant:
options: returning land to private ownership by individual peasants
selling the large state farms to foreign agricultural firms
letting peasants sell their surplus grain freely at market
merging peasant farms into state-run collective farms
questions.explanation: Peasants were forced to give up their land and livestock to collective farms that delivered grain to the state. Those who resisted, labelled kulaks, were deported or killed, and famine followed in 1932–33.

questions.stem: The Stakhanovite movement of 1935 was used by the Soviet regime to:
options: allow factory workers to elect their own managers and set their hours
reward peasants who chose to leave the collective farms
train artists to paint in the style of socialist realism
celebrate workers who far exceeded their output targets
questions.explanation: The miner Alexei Stakhanov was reported to have cut many times his quota of coal in one shift, and the regime used his example to push all workers to raise output. Workers did not gain control of their factories.

questions.stem: Strength Through Joy (KdF) in Nazi Germany:
options: censored film and radio for the Propaganda Ministry
organised cheap holidays and leisure for workers
negotiated pay rises in place of the banned trade unions
trained young men for service in the new air force
questions.explanation: KdF, part of the German Labour Front, offered concerts, sport and cruises to win workers' loyalty after independent trade unions were abolished in 1933. It did not bargain over wages, which the regime controlled.

questions.stem: The Nuremberg Laws of 1935:
options: ordered German Jews to be deported to camps in occupied Poland
began the boycott of Jewish shops and businesses
planned the murder of Europe's Jews at a secret conference
removed German citizenship from Jews and banned their marriage to non-Jews
questions.explanation: The Reich Citizenship Law made Jews subjects rather than citizens, and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honour banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and 'German-blooded' people. The boycott was in 1933 and the Wannsee Conference in 1942.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the escalation of Nazi persecution of Jews in the correct order?
options: Kristallnacht, boycott of Jewish shops, Nuremberg Laws, Wannsee Conference
boycott of Jewish shops, Kristallnacht, Nuremberg Laws, Wannsee Conference
boycott of Jewish shops, Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht, Wannsee Conference
Nuremberg Laws, boycott of Jewish shops, Wannsee Conference, Kristallnacht
questions.explanation: The boycott came in April 1933, the Nuremberg Laws in September 1935, Kristallnacht in November 1938 and the Wannsee Conference in January 1942. Each step moved from exclusion towards the organised murder of the Holocaust.

questions.stem: Kristallnacht, in November 1938, was:
options: the night Hitler had the leaders of the SA arrested and shot
the burning of 'un-German' books in university towns
the first deportation of German Jews to ghettos in Poland
a night of state-organised attacks on Jewish homes, shops and synagogues
questions.explanation: Nazi leaders used the shooting of a German diplomat in Paris as a pretext for violence across Germany and Austria, after which thousands of Jewish men were sent to concentration camps. The purge of the SA was the Night of the Long Knives in 1934.

questions.stem: Under Nazi rule, Sinti and Roma people were:
options: classed as racially alien, deported and murdered
exempted from the racial laws because most were Christian
allowed to emigrate freely if they gave up their property
treated only as 'asocials' and never classified by race
questions.explanation: The Nazis applied the Nuremberg race laws to Sinti and Roma, forced them into camps and murdered many in a genocide alongside the Holocaust. Their persecution was explicitly racial, not only a matter of 'asocial' labels.

questions.stem: Stalin's Great Purge of 1936–38 included:
options: free elections between rival socialist parties in the soviets
show trials of leading Bolsheviks such as Zinoviev and Bukharin
the end of War Communism and the start of the New Economic Policy
the abolition of the secret police and the labour camp system
questions.explanation: Old Bolsheviks confessed to invented crimes in public trials and were executed, while the NKVD arrested huge numbers of ordinary people. The New Economic Policy dates from 1921, and the Purge expanded the labour camps rather than closing them.

questions.stem: Which was a consequence of the Great Purge for the USSR?
options: Stalin's personal power was weakened by public criticism
the Communist Party was replaced by a multiparty parliament
the kulaks were given back their land as compensation
the Red Army lost much of its senior officer corps
questions.explanation: Marshal Tukhachevsky and a large share of the army's senior commanders were executed or imprisoned, weakening the Red Army before World War Two. The Purge strengthened Stalin's power by removing any possible rivals.

questions.stem: Japan's Peace Preservation Law of 1925 was used mainly to:
options: give every adult man the right to vote in elections
protect the right of trade unions to strike for higher wages
stop serving army officers from taking part in politics
suppress communists and others seen as a threat to the imperial system
questions.explanation: The law made it a crime to organise against the 'national polity' or private property, and the police used it against the left. Universal male suffrage was passed in the same year by a separate law, which is why the two are often confused.

questions.stem: The 'separate but equal' principle that upheld racial segregation in the southern USA came from:
options: the Thirteenth Amendment to the US Constitution
the Volstead Act passed by the US Congress
the Supreme Court's ruling in Plessy v Ferguson (1896)
the Supreme Court's ruling in Brown v Board of Education
questions.explanation: Plessy v Ferguson allowed states to keep races apart in public facilities so long as they were supposedly equal, the legal basis of Jim Crow laws. Brown v Board of Education overturned that principle for schools in 1954.

questions.stem: The Ku Klux Klan, revived in 1915, grew in the 1920s by targeting:
options: Protestant churches that supported Prohibition
returned soldiers who refused to rejoin the army
African Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants
white Protestant farmers in the Midwest and South
questions.explanation: The second Klan presented itself as defending white, Protestant, native-born America and spread well beyond the South. White Protestants were its members and supporters, not its targets.

questions.stem: During the Great Migration, millions of African Americans:
options: moved from the rural South to cities in the North and Midwest
returned to West Africa with the 'Back to Africa' movement
moved from northern cities to sharecropping farms in the South
settled in the western territories as homesteaders on new land
questions.explanation: Escaping Jim Crow laws and seeking factory work, African Americans moved to cities such as Chicago, Detroit and New York. This movement helped create the communities in which the Harlem Renaissance flourished.

questions.stem: The Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s is significant because it:
options: expressed African American identity and pride through the arts
ended racial segregation in New York's schools and theatres
was a federal arts program created as part of the New Deal
was led mainly by white patrons and writers from the South
questions.explanation: Writers such as Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston and musicians such as Duke Ellington celebrated Black culture and challenged racist stereotypes. Segregation and discrimination continued, so its significance was cultural rather than legal.

questions.stem: On 26 January 1938, the 150th anniversary of British colonisation, Aboriginal activists held:
options: the first Aboriginal Tent Embassy in Canberra
the Freedom Ride through western New South Wales
the walk-off by Gurindji workers at Wave Hill station
a Day of Mourning and Protest in Sydney
questions.explanation: The Aborigines Progressive Association and the Australian Aborigines' League, led by figures such as Jack Patten, William Ferguson and William Cooper, called for full citizenship rights. The Tent Embassy, Freedom Ride and Wave Hill walk-off came in the 1960s and 1970s.

questions.stem: In December 1938 Yorta Yorta man William Cooper led a delegation to the German consulate in Melbourne to protest against:
options: the bombing of Guernica by German aircraft in Spain
Germany's demand for the return of its Pacific colonies
the Nazi persecution of Jews after Kristallnacht
Germany's annexation of the Sudetenland in September
questions.explanation: Cooper's Australian Aborigines' League tried to deliver a resolution condemning the persecution of Jews, but the consulate refused to accept it. The protest linked the injustice faced by Aboriginal people with that faced by Jews in Germany.

questions.stem: Which best shows continuity in Australian society between Federation and the 1930s?
options: the federal vote was extended to all Aboriginal people across Australia
the dictation test was abolished and replaced by an entry permit system
women lost the right to vote in federal elections during the Depression
the White Australia policy stayed in force through the dictation test
questions.explanation: The Immigration Restriction Act and its dictation test continued to exclude non-European migrants throughout the period. Federal voting for all Aboriginal people came in 1962 and the dictation test was abolished in 1958, so both are changes from a later era.

questions.stem: Cubism, developed by Picasso and Braque before World War One, is known for:
options: showing objects from several viewpoints at once in geometric planes
painting dream images and the unconscious mind in realistic detail
celebrating speed, machines and the violence of modern warfare
using distorted forms and harsh colour to express strong emotion
questions.explanation: Cubism broke objects into flat, angular planes seen from different angles at once. Dream imagery belongs to Surrealism, machine worship to Futurism, and emotional distortion to Expressionism.

questions.stem: Marinetti's Futurist Manifesto of 1909 called war 'the world's only hygiene'. Futurism was later closely linked with:
options: Soviet socialist realism
the Harlem Renaissance
the Bauhaus school
Italian Fascism
questions.explanation: Futurism glorified speed, technology, youth and violence, and Marinetti and other Futurists became supporters of Mussolini's movement. Its love of war and nationalism suited Fascist ideas far more than socialist realism or the Bauhaus.

questions.stem: André Breton's Manifesto of Surrealism (1924) drew on Freud's ideas to argue that art should:
options: serve the state by showing workers building socialism
use the clean, functional shapes of machine production
record everyday life with complete photographic accuracy
release the hidden workings of the unconscious mind
questions.explanation: Breton defined Surrealism as 'psychic automatism', expressing thought free of reason's control, and placed great value on dreams. Showing workers building socialism was the aim of Soviet socialist realism.

questions.stem: German Expressionist films such as The Cabinet of Dr Caligari (1920) used:
options: bright colour and synchronised sound to impress audiences
happy endings that celebrated the new Weimar Republic
distorted sets and sharp shadows to show disturbed minds
documentary footage of real battles from the Western Front
questions.explanation: Caligari's painted, twisted sets express madness and unease, often read as reflecting the anxieties of post-war Germany. Synchronised sound did not arrive in feature films until the late 1920s.

questions.stem: The Bauhaus school, founded at Weimar in 1919 by Walter Gropius, is known for:
options: training painters in the official style of the Nazi regime
designing propaganda posters for the Soviet Communist Party
joining art, craft and industry in simple, functional design
reviving the decorated Gothic style of medieval cathedrals
questions.explanation: The Bauhaus taught that good design should suit mass production and serve its purpose, influencing furniture, architecture and typography worldwide. The Nazis condemned it, and it closed in 1933.

questions.stem: Art Deco takes its name from a 1925 Paris exhibition of decorative arts and is known for:
options: rough unfinished surfaces showing the lives of peasants
dream imagery such as clocks melting over tree branches
realistic and heroic paintings of industrial workers
bold geometric shapes and streamlined, luxurious forms
questions.explanation: Art Deco used zigzags, sunbursts and polished materials in buildings such as New York's Chrysler Building, expressing the glamour and confidence of the 1920s. Melting clocks belong to Dalí's Surrealism.

questions.stem: Socialist realism, made the official Soviet style in the 1930s, required artists to:
options: show a heroic, optimistic picture of socialist progress
experiment with abstract forms free from political content
follow the styles of Western modernist movements closely
depict the hardship and famine caused by collectivisation
questions.explanation: Art had to be easy to understand and show workers, peasants and Stalin building a better future. Abstract experiment was condemned as 'formalism', and showing famine would have been treated as anti-Soviet.

questions.stem: In 1936 Pravda attacked Shostakovich's opera Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk under the headline 'Muddle instead of music'. This best shows:
options: the popularity of American jazz among Soviet factory workers
the freedom of Soviet critics to judge new art independently
Shostakovich's open campaign against Stalin's leadership
the Soviet state's control over what counted as acceptable art
questions.explanation: Pravda was the Communist Party's newspaper, and the attack, which followed Stalin's visit to the opera, warned all composers to follow the party line. An unsigned editorial in the party paper is evidence of state control, not of independent criticism.

questions.stem: The Nazi 'Degenerate Art' exhibition of 1937 in Munich:
options: raised money for the Winter Relief to help the unemployed
mocked modernist works to turn the public against them
celebrated the Bauhaus as a model of German industrial design
displayed only paintings by Jewish artists made after 1933
questions.explanation: Works by Expressionists and other modernists were hung chaotically with insulting labels, while a nearby exhibition displayed approved 'German' art. The regime aimed to show that modern art was a sign of racial and moral decay.

questions.stem: On 10 May 1933, Nazi students in German university towns:
options: founded the Reich Ministry of Propaganda under Goebbels
burned books judged 'un-German', including works by Jewish writers
marched in protest against Hitler's appointment as Chancellor
voted to make the Hitler Youth compulsory for all students
questions.explanation: Students and Nazi officials burned books by Jewish, pacifist and left-wing authors, with Goebbels speaking at the Berlin bonfire. The Propaganda Ministry had already been created in March 1933.

questions.stem: Why did the Nazi regime promote the cheap People's Receiver (Volksempfänger) radio?
options: to bring Nazi broadcasts into as many homes as possible
to let Germans listen freely to the BBC and other foreign stations
to raise money for rearmament from the profits on radio sales
to replace newspapers, which were all closed down in 1933
questions.explanation: Goebbels saw radio as the most powerful propaganda tool, and the cheap set made Hitler's speeches available to millions. Listening to foreign stations became a crime once war began, and newspapers continued under Nazi control.

questions.stem: Leni Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will (1935), filmed at the 1934 Nuremberg Rally, is significant as:
options: a documentary exposing the violence of the SA in the streets
a Hollywood satire mocking Hitler and his followers
a film banned by Goebbels for criticising the regime
propaganda presenting Hitler as the leader of a united nation
questions.explanation: Through dramatic camera angles and vast crowds, the film presents Hitler and the Party as the embodiment of Germany. The Hollywood satire of Hitler was Chaplin's The Great Dictator of 1940.

questions.stem: Charlie Chaplin's film Modern Times (1936) is best read as a comment on:
options: the dehumanising effects of mechanised factory work
the glamour and wealth of Hollywood's jazz age stars
the heroism of Soviet workers meeting their targets
the success of the New Deal in ending unemployment
questions.explanation: Chaplin's Tramp is swallowed by machinery on a speeding production line, satirising industrial life and the hardship of the Depression. The film shows poverty and unemployment continuing, not ended.

questions.stem: Erich Maria Remarque's novel All Quiet on the Western Front (1929) was burned by the Nazis mainly because it:
options: praised the Treaty of Versailles as a fair and lasting peace
was written in English by a British soldier about Germany
called openly for a communist revolution in Germany
showed the war as senseless suffering, not heroic sacrifice
questions.explanation: Remarque, a German veteran, showed young soldiers destroyed by the war, which contradicted the Nazi glorification of combat. The novel is anti-war rather than political in a party sense.

questions.stem: A student uses Dorothea Lange's photograph Migrant Mother (1936), taken for a New Deal agency, as evidence of rural poverty. Which limitation should the student consider?
options: it was painted from memory rather than photographed on the spot
it was made for an agency seeking public support for its relief work
it was taken several decades after the Great Depression had ended
it shows a scene from the Depression in rural Australia, not the USA
questions.explanation: Lange worked for a government agency whose photographs were meant to build sympathy for relief programs, so its purpose shaped what was shown. It remains valuable evidence of hardship, but it is a chosen image rather than a neutral record.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the 1920s brought lasting change for American women. Which evidence would most weaken this argument?
options: flappers adopted shorter hair and new fashions in the cities
many young women took jobs in offices and department stores
most married women still did not work outside the home
women gained the federal vote under the Nineteenth Amendment
questions.explanation: If most married women's lives stayed centred on the home, the change was limited and mostly affected young, urban women. The other three pieces of evidence support the argument for change rather than weakening it.
